tasks.locator: Methods › 2.1. Participants and procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs, and 2.1.1.1. Crime (p. 2); Methods › 2.1.2. Design and statistical analysis, Table 1 (violent crime row and notes) and Results › 3.2. Changes in crime during periods of methamphetamine use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3)
tasks.extracted: MATES cohort (Sydney and Brisbane, recruited 2006–2007, followed to 2010): 469 people with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence at entry (from 400 people entering community treatment and 101 recruited through needle and syringe programmes and outreach), interviewed about the past month at baseline, 3 months (379), 12 months (357) and 3 years (315); 1,518 person-months for violent crime. Violent crime (any crime involving violence, such as violence in a robbery or assault, self-reported on the Opiate Treatment Index crime scale): 19 of 593 months without methamphetamine use (3%) against 113 of 927 months with use (12%). Within-person odds ratios, months with use against months without: unadjusted 8.2 (95% CI 4.2–15.9); adjusted for time-varying age, income, unemployment and unstable accommodation 5.3 (2.6–10.7); also adjusted for alcohol and cannabis (0, 1–15, 16+ days) and any cocaine, heroin and ecstasy use 3.4 (1.5–8.0), p = 0.005.

tasks.locator: Methods › 2.1.2. Design and statistical analysis and Results › 3.1. Characteristics of the sample, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Results › 3.2, 3rd paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4) and Fig. 1 (p. 4); Discussion › 4.1. Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 5)
tasks.extracted: The analysis was exploratory and not pre-registered; the methods describe random-effects logistic models with a random intercept and use of the fixed-effects option for the within-person effect, and the number of participants contributing to each estimate is not reported. Use and crime were reported for the same month in the same interview; treatment received and imprisonment during follow-up are not covariates, and tobacco is not among the covariates. Methamphetamine was used in 61% of observed months (median 10 days in months of use; injection the main route in 80%). Crime rose with days of use in unadjusted percentages pooled across months (Fig. 1: no use, 1–15 and 16+ days); the adjusted dose estimates are only in a supplementary table, not available. The authors state that crime was self-reported, not convictions; that the direction of the same-month relationship could be disputed; that few participants committed crime in months without use, giving wide confidence limits, and small numbers limit the dose findings; and that the results apply to people dependent on methamphetamine, most of whom injected, not to recreational use. Editors' reading of Fig. 1 (no values printed): violent crime in about 3%, 9% and 19% of months with no use, 1–15 days and 16+ days of use.

tasks.locator: Author list, Abstract (Conclusions) and Introduction, 1st paragraph (p. 1); Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 2); Discussion, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (p. 4); reference list (p. 6)
tasks.extracted: The authors conclude that use was associated with significant increases in crime beyond premorbid risk and that crime is a likely social consequence of use; in the discussion they call the evidence robust and say that violent crime among people who use methamphetamine is not only a consequence of pre-existing risk, while noting that they cannot tell whether the violence was instrumental (for example robbery) or expressive (for example domestic assault). They state that they applied the same within-person approach earlier to hostility and psychotic symptoms (McKetin et al., 2014 and 2013b). Three of the four authors of the birth-cohort study (Foulds, Boden, McKetin; Foulds et al., 2020) and four authors of the 2019 review (McKetin, Foulds, Degenhardt, Farrell) are authors of this paper.

tasks.page: p. 2 of the Supporting Online Material
tasks.locator: Supporting Online Material › Materials and Methods › Study sample, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Recruited through advertisements and treatment services in East Anglia, UK; all assessed with the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV. Sibling pairs had the same biological parents; one met DSM-IV-TR criteria for cocaine or amphetamine dependence and the other had no personal history of substance dependence except nicotine; controls had no personal or family history of drug or alcohol dependence; all were aged 18–55. Of 154 enrolled, 150 completed (three groups of 50); MRI scans were unavailable for three dependent participants and one sibling, leaving 47, 49 and 50. All dependent participants met DSM-IV-TR criteria for stimulant dependence, 94% for cocaine and 6% for amphetamines (which amphetamines is not stated; methamphetamine is not mentioned); they had used stimulants for a mean of 16.3 years (SD 7.6) from a mean age of 16.5 (SD 2.8); urine was positive for stimulants in all but three; most also met criteria for dependence on another substance (opiates 55%, alcohol 26%, cannabis 9%). Siblings and controls had very low drug and alcohol screening scores and drug-negative urine.

tasks.page: pp. 2–3, 8 of the Supporting Online Material
tasks.locator: Supporting Online Material › Materials and Methods › Study sample, 4th paragraph (p. 2, continuing on p. 3) and 5th paragraph, and Statistical analysis (p. 3); Table S1 (p. 8)
tasks.extracted: Table S1 (50 controls, 49 non-dependent siblings, 47 dependent siblings): men 64%, 51% and 92% (chi-square 19.0, P < 0.001); age 32.8, 32.6 and 34.5 years (P = 0.702); verbal IQ 112.3, 108.9 and 110.3 (P = 0.143); education 12.6, 12.1 and 11.6 years (P = 0.062); current smokers 12%, 55% and 94% (chi-square 71.8); upbringing shared until age 10 for 90% and 92% of the two sibling groups and until 15 for 75% and 89%; AUDIT 3.3, 3.9 and 11.4; DAST-20 0.0 and 0.5 in controls and non-dependent siblings. Alcohol use did not differ between non-dependent siblings and controls (t(70.9) = −0.72, P = 0.472). Sex was a covariate in the analyses of demographic and stop-signal data. The dependent participants were tested while still using stimulants, not asked to abstain and screened only for intoxication severe enough to incapacitate them; alcohol was not breathalysed.

tasks.page: pp. 4–5, 9 of the Supporting Online Material
tasks.locator: Supporting Online Material › Materials and Methods › MRI data processing and analyses (p. 4); DTI data processing and analyses, 1st paragraph (p. 4, continuing on p. 5) and 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Table S2 (p. 9)
tasks.extracted: Grey matter was analysed in 50 controls, 47 dependent participants and 49 siblings, and FA in 50, 46 and 49 (one dependent participant could not tolerate the full session). Grey-matter maps were compared with the controls by permutation tests at a cluster-level threshold of one expected false-positive cluster per map (cluster-wise P = 9 × 10⁻⁴ for siblings and 8 × 10⁻⁴ for dependent participants), giving four clusters for the siblings and eight for the dependent participants; the voxels in both lay in three regions, and analyses restricted to men or to women did not change the results. FA: voxel-wise permutation tests with threshold-free cluster enhancement and 5000 permutations, corrected at P < 0.05; mean FA in the significant skeleton was then compared in SPSS. Table S2 (means, SD): FA across the 24,934 skeleton voxels that differed between groups 0.55 (0.02) in controls, 0.53 (0.02) in siblings and 0.52 (0.02) in dependent participants; grey matter in the left amygdala cluster (984 mm³) 0.76, 0.81 and 0.83 (0.07), left putamen (560 mm³) 0.34, 0.38 and 0.38 (0.05–0.06), left postcentral gyrus (1,152 mm³) 0.89, 0.75 and 0.74 (0.11–0.12). Editors' calculation: standardized differences from controls about 0.7, 0.7 and 1.2 SD (siblings) and 1.0, 0.8 and 1.3 SD (dependent participants) for the three grey-matter clusters; all inflated, because the values are means over voxels selected for differing.

tasks.page: pp. 5–7, 10 of the Supporting Online Material
tasks.locator: Supporting Online Material › Materials and Methods › Assessment of familiality (p. 5); Effects of tobacco smoking on gray and white matter, 1st paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 6); Fig. S1 legend (p. 6); Fig. S2 legend (p. 7); Table S3 (p. 10)
tasks.extracted: Familiality: the variance of within-pair differences was compared with its distribution when each dependent participant was paired at random with an unrelated sibling (100,000 re-pairings), as a one-tailed test; no adjustment for age or sex is described. Smoking: a re-analysis restricted to non-smoking controls and siblings (numbers not given) kept the amygdala, putamen and postcentral differences significant (Fig. S1, no statistics); no smoking analysis is described for white matter or the stop-signal task, although the section heading names white matter; the sentence after the re-analysis says, as printed, that the siblings' differences might instead be due to tobacco, the opposite of the authors' argument. The supplement labels the shared medial temporal cluster amygdala/hippocampus in its text and in Table S3 (peak −22, −6, −16) but amygdala in Table S2 and Fig. S1, and names no orbitofrontal or anterior insular cluster. Duration of use: maps only (Fig. S2): FA regions negatively correlated with years of stimulant use, less extensive than the familial effect, and grey-matter regions negatively correlated with duration, in places different from the shared clusters; no statistics, region names, correction or adjustment for age are given.
